Apple___Apple_scab.summary: Fungal infection causing olive-green to dark brown velvety scabs on leaves and fruit, causing premature leaf fall.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on upper leaf surfaces that turn dark brown or black
Puckered, curled leaves that yellow and drop prematurely
Scabby, corky dark lesions on fruit that may crack open as fruit grows
immediate_actions: Rake up, collect, and burn or bury fallen infected leaves to stop ascospore release
Prune dense canopy branches during dry weather to increase airflow and sunlight penetration

organic_cultural: Apply neem oil (3-5 ml/L) or wettable sulfur as a preventive spray before bud break
Keep the orchard floor clean and well-mowed to reduce humidity under the trees

chemical.note: Protective spray; apply at green tip stage and repeat at pink bud stage
Curative spray; apply within 72 hours of an infection rain event

prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars adapted to your region
Ensure wide tree spacing to allow rapid canopy drying after rain
Apply urea (5%) to fallen leaves in autumn to accelerate leaf decomposition
Apple___Apple_scab.when_to_seek_help: Contact your local horticulture officer if scabs appear on over 20% of your young fruitlets despite preventive spraying.

Apple___Black_rot.summary: Fungal disease causing frog-eye circular leaf spots, limb cankers, and firm, decaying black rot on fruit.
symptoms: Small purple leaf spots that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers ('frog-eye' spots)
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on bark and larger limbs with cracked borders
Firm, dark rotting rings on ripening fruit that dry into shriveled black mummies
immediate_actions: Prune out dead wood, cankered twigs, and mummified fruit hanging on the tree
Dispose of all pruned diseased wood and fallen mummies away from the orchard

organic_cultural: Sterilize pruning shears with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach solution between cuts
Avoid tree stress by mulching and watering during prolonged dry spells

chemical.note: Apply from petal fall through summer cover sprays at 10-14 day intervals

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Rotational fungicide for canker and summer rot suppression

prevention: Prevent bark damage from mowers, pruning tools, and insect borers
Maintain balanced tree nutrition and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer
Remove nearby wild brambles or dead hardwood trees that harbor the fungus
Apple___Black_rot.when_to_seek_help: Seek guidance from an agricultural university extension if major scaffold limbs show expanding trunk cankers.

Tube-like fungal structures on the lower leaf surface that release powdery orange spores

organic_cultural: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties such as Enterprise, Liberty, or Freedom

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Systemic fungicide applied at early infection timing

prevention: Select disease-resistant rootstocks and scion varieties
Maintain spatial separation between apple orchards and juniper trees
Keep orchard canopies well-pruned for rapid leaf drying after morning dew

Avoid continuous maize cultivation in the same field

symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target board') on older leaves
Surrounding leaf tissue turns chlorotic yellow, leading to premature leaf drop
Sunken, dark, leathery lesions at the stem end of developing tomato fruits
immediate_actions: Prune off the lowest 30 cm of foliage once plants are established to prevent soil contact
Mulch around the base of plants with straw or plastic film to prevent rain splash

organic_cultural: Water at soil level with drip irrigation; avoid overhead sprinklers
Rotate away from solanaceous crops (potato, pepper, eggplant) for at least 2 seasons

chemical.note: Preventive spray every 10-14 days starting at first cluster flowering
Apply at first sign of lower leaf spotting

prevention: Stake or trellis tomato vines to keep foliage upright and dry
Space plants at least 50-60 cm apart to ensure airflow
Destroy solanaceous crop residues and weeds immediately after harvest
Tomato___Early_blight.when_to_seek_help: Consult a village agricultural officer if target spots spread to upper foliage near fruit clusters.

Tomato___Late_blight.summary: Fast-spreading disease under cool, damp conditions causing large water-soaked greasy patches and white fungal fuzz.
symptoms: Rapidly expanding water-soaked greasy dark greenish-brown lesions on leaves and stems
White delicate fungal mold on the underside of affected leaves during high humidity
Firm, greasy, olive-brown sunken decay on green and ripe tomato fruits
immediate_actions: Remove and bag severely infected plants immediately; do not add to compost piles
Ensure high air circulation by staking, trellising, and pruning suckers

organic_cultural: Avoid planting tomatoes downwind or adjacent to late-blight infected potato fields
Select late blight-tolerant hybrid tomato varieties

chemical.note: Preventive cover spray prior to rainy, cool spells
Curative systemic spray when early symptoms are identified in the vicinity

prevention: Plant late-blight resistant tomato cultivars
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation beneath plastic mulch
Follow local weather-based disease forecast advisories
Tomato___Late_blight.when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate advice from your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra, as late blight can destroy an entire field within days.

sources.name: TNAU Agritech Portal - Tomato Late Blight
PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank - Late Blight of Tomato

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.summary: Fungal disease common in humid greenhouses causing pale green/yellow leaf patches with velvety olive-green mold below.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish blotches on upper leaf surfaces with indistinct margins
Dense, velvety olive-green to brownish fungal mold growth on the corresponding lower leaf surface
Infected leaves curl, wither, and drop prematurely in high relative humidity (>85%)
immediate_actions: Increase greenhouse ventilation and turn on exhaust fans to lower relative humidity below 80%
Space tomato plants generously and prune bottom leaves to facilitate air movement

organic_cultural: Water early in the morning and avoid splashing water onto foliage
Grow leaf-mold resistant greenhouse tomato hybrids

chemical.note: Thorough foliar spray ensuring complete coverage of leaf undersides

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Systemic triazole fungicide for protected cultivation

prevention: Maintain greenhouse relative humidity below 85% with adequate night-time ventilation
Disinfect polyhouse structures and planting stakes between crop cycles
Use drip irrigation under mulch to prevent standing water inside polyhouses
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.when_to_seek_help: Contact a protected-cultivation specialist if olive mold covers more than 20% of the greenhouse canopy.

PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank - Tomato Leaf Mould

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Fungal leaf disease characterized by numerous small circular spots with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins.
symptoms: Numerous small (2-3 mm) circular spots with grayish-white centers and distinct dark brown margins
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) clearly visible inside the center of mature spots
Rapid leaf yellowing and defoliation progressing strictly from oldest bottom leaves upwards
immediate_actions: Pick off and destroy infected lower leaves at first notice before disease reaches fruit clusters
Apply organic mulch around tomato bases to prevent rain-splash from soil

organic_cultural: Practice 3-year crop rotation without solanaceous crops
Keep field weed-free; eliminate solanaceous weeds like black nightshade

chemical.note: Foliar spray on bottom leaves every 7-10 days during warm, rainy weather
Broad-spectrum protectant spray

prevention: Mulch beds heavily to create a barrier between soil-borne spores and lower leaves
Stake and prune indeterminate tomatoes to maintain upright air circulation
Destroy all tomato crop vines immediately after final harvest
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.when_to_seek_help: Consult your local agriculture officer if spots progress more than halfway up the plant canopy.

PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank - Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.summary: Microscopic sap-feeding arachnid pests causing fine yellow stippling, bronzing, and delicate silk webbing on leaves.
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white speckles and stippling across the upper leaf surface
Fine, silky webbing visible on leaf undersides, growing tips, and flower clusters in heavy infestations
Leaves turn bronze or yellow, dry up, and plants appear dusty and stunted
immediate_actions: Wash down foliage undersides with a strong stream of water to dislodge mites and webs
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids which kill beneficial predatory mites and cause pest flares

organic_cultural: Spray neem oil (5 ml per liter of water with soap) or insecticidal soap solution
Conserve or release natural predatory mites (*Phytoseiulus persimilis*)

chemical.note: Thorough foliar spray targeting leaf undersides where mites feed

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Contact acaricide; alternate modes of action to prevent resistance

prevention: Avoid dusty field conditions; keep dirt farm roads watered or mulched near tomato plots
Avoid water-stressing tomato crops, as drought conditions accelerate mite reproduction
Inspect borders and weeds regularly for initial mite hotspots
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.when_to_seek_help: Consult a pest management officer if webbing envelopes growing tips and flower clusters.

Tomato___Target_Spot.summary: Fungal disease causing brown circular lesions with concentric rings and sunken, crater-like lesions on green fruit.
symptoms: Small brown pinpoint spots that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers and dark concentric rings
Spots on leaves and stems often have yellow chlorotic halos, causing extensive defoliation
Small, brown, sunken spots on tomato fruit that expand into large deep craters
immediate_actions: Increase spacing between plants and stake vines securely off the ground
Prune lower foliage to maintain good air circulation and rapid leaf drying

organic_cultural: Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip lines under plastic mulch
Rotate with non-susceptible crops like maize, sorghum, or grasses

chemical.note: Spray at first appearance of symptoms and repeat after 12-14 days

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Protectant fungicide; follow label spray intervals

prevention: Avoid planting tomatoes near older infected cucurbit, pepper, or tomato plantings
Maintain uniform plant nutrition and avoid excessive nitrogen
Ensure rapid field drainage during monsoon periods
Tomato___Target_Spot.when_to_seek_help: Contact your local agricultural extension service if target spot lesions appear on immature green fruit.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: Destructive virus spread by whiteflies resulting in severe stunting, upward leaf curling, yellow margins, and flower drop.
symptoms: Pronounced upward curling and cupping of leaflets
Interveinal yellowing (chlorosis) along leaflet margins with reduced leaf size
Severe plant stunting, bushy erect appearance, and flower drop preventing fruit set
immediate_actions: Rogue out and destroy virus-infected plants immediately to prevent whiteflies from acquiring and spreading the virus
Install yellow sticky traps (15-20 traps per acre) in and around the field to monitor and trap whiteflies

organic_cultural: Erect insect-proof 40-50 mesh nylon netting in nurseries
Plant border crops of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet (2-3 rows) around tomato fields as physical barriers

chemical.note: Spray to control whitefly vector population; no chemical cures the virus itself

chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Systemic insecticide for vector control; rotate chemicals to manage resistance

prevention: Grow TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g. varieties carrying Ty genes)
Raise seedlings under 40-mesh insect-proof netting to ensure virus-free transplants
Eliminate weed hosts like Datura, Parthenium, and wild Solanum around field borders
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.when_to_seek_help: Contact your district agriculture officer if whitefly populations surge despite sticky traps and systemic sprays.

PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: Extremely stable mechanically transmitted virus creating light/dark green mottled mosaic patterns and leaf distortion.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves with blistered or puckered surfaces
Leaf distortion, curling, and in severe cases narrow 'shoestring' or 'fern-like' leaves
Stunted plant growth with brown internal necrotic browning inside fruits
immediate_actions: Carefully rogue out and destroy infected plants; do NOT compost them
Wash hands with soap and water or skimmed milk before touching healthy plants, especially after handling tobacco

organic_cultural: Disinfect all pruning knives, stakes, and tools in 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or 20% household bleach
Plant certified ToMV-resistant tomato varieties (designated with Tm-2/Tm-2^2 resistance)

chemical.active_ingredient: None (Viral disease - chemical control is ineffective)
chemical.dosage: Follow the product label and local advisory
chemical.note: Antibiotics and synthetic pesticides cannot cure plant viruses. Focus strictly on sanitation and tool hygiene.

prevention: Use certified virus-free seed treated with 10% trisodium phosphate or heat treatment
Prohibit smoking or tobacco handling near greenhouses and tomato fields
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least 2 seasons
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.when_to_seek_help: Consult a plant virologist or KVK scientist if mosaic symptoms appear widely in a commercial greenhouse crop.

PlantwisePlus Knowledge Bank - Tomato Mosaic Virus

Tomato___healthy.summary: Your tomato plant leaves look healthy, lush green, and free from blight or virus symptoms.
prevention: Stake and prune vines regularly to prevent leaves from touching damp soil
Apply drip irrigation under mulch to keep foliage dry and reduce disease pressure
Scout lower leaves twice weekly for early signs of fungal leaf spots
Tomato___healthy.when_to_seek_help: Consult a village agriculture assistant if leaves develop dark spots, yellow margins, or powdery growth.
